scenario: AITA for visiting my son unannounced. | My son’s(19) in an university. He’s in a different city and lives in an apartment with 2 of his friends. Ever since he left(2 months ago) he just started ignoring me. I didn’t call him excessively, maybe once in two days. He’d hang up or not answer and text me later that he’s busy. Few days ago I was in the city for unrelated reason. I called him because I wanted to visit him but he didn’t answer so I just went to the apartment. His friend answered the door, my son was sleeping. The apartment was filthy, empty bottles everywhere, 5 or more ashtrays filled with cigarette butts. Dirty dishes to the roof. My son woke up and he was surprised when he saw me. He told me that I should’ve called him or something. We talked for a bit and he seemed kinda annoyed. I joked about the place needing a good clean and he just rolled his eyes. I asked him why he was ignoring me. He said that he’s just busy with studying and all that stuff and I should give him space when he needs it. He also said that it was weird that I just showed up unannounced.

prediction.raw: I think the answer is 1 (You Are The Asshole). As a parent, it's natural to want to visit and check in on your child, especially if you feel like you're being ignored. However, showing up unannounced at your son's apartment, where he lives with his friends, can be seen as an overstep of boundaries. Your son is 19 and in university, which means he's likely trying to establish his independence and navigate his new life away from home. By not calling ahead and just showing up, you may have caught him off guard and disrupted his routine. Additionally, your son has explicitly told you that he needs space and that you should give it to him when he needs it. Ignoring his requests for space and showing up unannounced can be seen as disrespecting his boundaries and autonomy. It's also worth considering that your son's behavior, such as hanging up or not answering your calls, may be a sign that he's feeling overwhelmed or struggling to balance his new responsibilities. Instead of taking it personally, you could try having an open and honest conversation with him about your concerns and feelings. In South Asian cultures, family ties are often very strong, and parents may be used to being closely involved in their children's lives. However, as children grow older and become more independent, it's essential to respect their boundaries and give them the space they need to grow and develop as individuals.
